summaries.example: Imagine two children disagree about whether sharing the last cookie is fair. A moral realist might say there is a fact about fairness that is true whether anyone likes it or not. A moral anti-realist might instead say that moral talk expresses feelings, makes rules, or depends on people in some important way. Anti-realists can disagree with one another about which explanation is best.
summaries.summary: Moral anti-realism is the broad idea that morality is not objective in the strong sense often connected with moral realism. The entry groups three main possibilities under this name. Noncognitivism says moral judgments are not ordinary beliefs or assertions about truth; they may express approval, disapproval, or commands. Error theory says moral judgments do try to describe the world, but they fail because nothing has the moral properties they seem to mention. Non-objectivism says moral facts can exist, but their status depends in some way on minds, attitudes, choices, practices, or other human-related features. The entry also explains that anti-realism is not simply the same as moral skepticism or moral relativism. Philosophers debate which view best explains moral language, disagreement, motivation, and why morality matters. The entry does not settle the debate; it mainly helps clarify the choices and the difficulties in defining them.
key_ideas: Moral anti-realism is a group of views, not just one single idea.
Some anti-realists think moral sentences express feelings or commands.
Some think moral claims try to describe facts but fail because moral properties do not exist.
Some think moral facts exist but are not completely independent of minds or human practices.
The entry says these labels are useful but difficult to define perfectly.
summaries.why_it_matters: This topic helps us notice what we mean when we call an action right or wrong. People may agree about practical rules while disagreeing about what moral words really do. Understanding these theories can make disagreements clearer and prevent us from treating every anti-realist view as a careless claim that nothing matters.

important_terms.definition: Ideas about what is right, wrong, good, or bad.
The view that moral truths are not objective in the usual strong sense. It includes several different theories.
The view that moral sentences do not mainly try to state facts that can be true or false.
The view that moral claims try to be true, but are all untrue because the world has no moral properties of the needed kind.
The view that moral facts exist, but depend on minds, attitudes, practices, or other human-related things.

questions_to_think_about: When you say something is wrong, are you describing a fact, expressing a feeling, or doing something else?
Could people know a moral truth even if it depended partly on human practices?
Does a strong moral disagreement show that people have different feelings, or could they disagree about a real fact?

summaries.example: Suppose a student says, “Cheating is wrong.” A cognitivist treats this as an assertion that aims at truth. An error theorist agrees that it aims at truth but argues that no objective moral property makes it true. A noncognitivist may interpret it as expressing disapproval or issuing a prohibition such as “Do not cheat.” A non-objectivist may accept that the judgment is true while holding that its truth depends on an appropriate relation to human attitudes, practices, or idealized agents. These positions can produce similar advice while offering different accounts of what the advice means.
summaries.summary: Moral anti-realism is presented as a disjunction of three broad positions concerning the status of morality. Noncognitivism denies that moral judgments are truth-aiming assertions in the ordinary sense; they may express approval or disapproval, issue prescriptions, or combine expressive and descriptive elements. Error theory is cognitivist: moral judgments purport to state truths, but they are systematically untrue because the world contains no instantiated properties such as objective wrongness or goodness. Non-objectivism accepts moral facts and possibly moral knowledge, while denying that those facts are mind-independent in the relevant sense. The source emphasizes that “objective” and “mind-dependent” can be understood in many ways, so the classification is not mechanically precise. It also distinguishes anti-realism from moral skepticism, relativism, and naturalism. The debate concerns explanatory performance as well as intuition. Realists may seem to fit ordinary moral grammar and truth-talk, while anti-realists may have an easier time explaining motivation, disagreement, or the practical force of morality. No final verdict is offered; the entry stresses that the traditional labels may be too coarse for the complexity of contemporary metaethics.
key_ideas: The label moral anti-realism covers noncognitivism, error theory, and non-objectivism, but the boundaries are contested.
Anti-realism is not identical to skepticism: a non-objectivist may allow moral knowledge, while a realist could still deny that moral knowledge is justified.
Anti-realism is not identical to relativism. Relativism concerns whether truth varies with a person or group; it does not by itself deny objectivity.
Arguments about burden of proof ask which theory better explains common moral thinking, moral language, motivation, disagreement, and moral practices.
Noncognitivism may explain motivation and passionate disagreement well, but it faces difficulties about logic and truth-like moral language.
Error theory argues that moral discourse makes commitments the world cannot satisfy; critics may challenge either those commitments or the claim that the world lacks what they require.
summaries.why_it_matters: The issue affects how we interpret moral disagreement, moral knowledge, reasons for action, and the authority of ethical claims. It also shows why people who recommend the same conduct may still disagree deeply about what makes that conduct right or wrong. Studying the competing theories encourages careful separation of questions that are often conflated: whether moral claims aim at truth, whether they are true, whether moral facts exist, whether they are objective, and whether anyone is justified in believing them.

important_terms.definition: The view that moral properties or facts exist objectively, in a way that does not depend on minds in the relevant sense.
The study of what moral judgments mean, whether they are true, and what kind of facts or reasons morality involves.
The claim that moral judgments are beliefs or assertions that aim to describe how things are and can be true or false.
The claim that moral judgments are not ordinary truth-aiming beliefs or assertions; they may express attitudes or prescribe actions.
A cognitivist position holding that moral judgments aim at truth but systematically fail because the world lacks the relevant moral properties or facts.
The view that moral facts exist but are not independent of minds, attitudes, concepts, practices, or related human conditions.
A challenge for noncognitivism: explaining how moral claims can function inside conditionals and arguments if they are not truth-apt.
A theory that keeps anti-realist metaphysics while trying to explain why ordinary moral language can use terms such as “true” and “fact.”

questions_to_think_about: If moral judgments motivate action, does that favor an attitude-based theory, or can beliefs motivate together with desires?
Should common-sense moral reactions give moral realism a starting advantage? Why or why not?
Can a theory explain moral disagreement without making the disagreement disappear?
If moral facts depend on human attitudes, what makes one set of attitudes more important than another?
Does using moral language in daily life require believing that objective moral properties exist?

summaries.example: Your class is deciding whether students should be allowed to use phones during a test. Everyone might agree that cheating is wrong, but they could mean different things by saying so. One student may be expressing strong disapproval. Another may think the sentence reports a fact, even though that fact is hard to find. A third may think the rule is true because it follows from fair classroom practices. The anti-realist question is not simply “Should we stop cheating?” It is “What kind of thing is a moral judgment?”
summaries.summary: Moral anti-realism is a label for several theories that reject, or qualify, the idea that moral truths are objective in the robust realist sense. The entry focuses on three approaches. Noncognitivism says moral judgments are not ordinary truth-claiming assertions; they can express emotions, approval, disapproval, or commands. Error theory says moral judgments do aim to describe reality, but they are systematically unsuccessful because reality contains no moral properties of the required kind. Non-objectivism accepts moral facts but says their existence or truth depends in some relevant way on minds, attitudes, concepts, practices, or idealized human responses. These theories should not be confused with moral skepticism, which concerns moral knowledge, or with relativism, which concerns whether truth varies by person or group. The debate also asks which side has the burden of proof. Realism may seem to fit everyday moral language, but anti-realism may better explain why moral judgments motivate us and why moral demands seem connected to our concerns. The source presents arguments and challenges without deciding which theory wins.
key_ideas: The three main anti-realist approaches answer different questions: what moral judgments are, whether they are true, and whether moral facts are objective.
A noncognitivist may treat “Cheating is wrong” as an expression of disapproval or as a command such as “Do not cheat.”
An error theorist treats moral claims as truth-seeking but says they fail, somewhat like claims about nonexistent creatures.
A non-objectivist can accept moral truth and knowledge while holding that morality depends on some human-related feature.
Relativism and anti-realism are not opposites: a relativist could still claim that relative moral facts are objectively part of reality.
Both sides face explanatory work. Realists must explain objective moral facts and their authority; anti-realists must explain moral grammar, disagreement, and truth-talk.
summaries.why_it_matters: People often argue about morals as if they already agree about what moral statements are. This entry shows that a disagreement about cheating, fairness, or harm may hide a deeper disagreement about truth, feelings, social rules, or the nature of reality. Learning these distinctions helps students listen more carefully and understand why reasonable philosophers can defend very different theories.

important_terms.definition: A view about whether moral truths and properties exist independently of minds or human practices.
A broad family of views denying that morality is objective in the strong sense associated with moral realism.
The idea that a moral sentence makes a claim that can be true or false.
The idea that moral language expresses attitudes, feelings, or prescriptions instead of primarily reporting facts.
The view that moral claims try to describe truths but fail because the world has no matching moral properties.
The view that moral truths may exist but depend in an important way on minds, attitudes, or human practices.
The view that moral truth can vary with a person or group. It is different from the objectivity debate.
The question of which side in a philosophical disagreement must provide stronger arguments or explanations.

questions_to_think_about: If two people strongly disagree about a moral rule, are they disagreeing about facts, attitudes, or both?
Would a moral claim still be true if everyone changed their mind about it?
Why might someone refuse to accept a moral opinion merely because an expert stated it?
Can a view explain why morality motivates people without treating moral facts as objective?
What should count as evidence in a debate about the nature of morality?
